summary: Describes RSVP-TE signaling extensions for protecting and restoring just a segment of a GMPLS label switched path. It complements the end-to-end recovery extensions of RFC 4872 and discusses how they interact. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Instead of finding a new road for the whole trip, you only fix the broken part. This note explains how the network repairs just one stretch of a path.

questions: how to protect part of an lsp
what is a secondary explicit route object
what is a branch node and merge node in gmpls
difference between segment and end-to-end lsp protection
subtitle: How to protect or restore just one stretch of a GMPLS label switched path instead of the whole route.

tldr.problem: End-to-end recovery (RFC 4872) needs a second path between the same ingress and egress nodes, which is not always possible, and fast reroute (RFC 4090) does not cover the full set of recovery types or most non-packet technologies.
tldr.mechanism: A segment recovery LSP is signaled as an independent LSP from a branch node to a merge node, tied to the protected LSP with ASSOCIATION objects. New Secondary Explicit Route and Secondary Record Route objects name and record the segments, or PROTECTION object flags let nodes find branch and merge points dynamically.
tldr.outcome: The full set of RFC 4872 recovery types works on a portion of an LSP, with overlapping and nested protection allowed. The RFC also changes how NOTIFY_REQUEST objects are handled, and it is updated by RFC 9270.

today: RFC 4873 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3473 and RFC 4872, and it has itself been updated by RFC 9270. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Recover Only a Segment
sections.content:
RFC 4872 defines GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling for several types of recovery: 1+1 unidirectional and bidirectional protection, LSP protection with extra-traffic, pre-planned re-routing without extra-traffic (including shared mesh), and full LSP re-routing. In every case recovery is end-to-end: the protected LSP and the protecting LSP share the same ingress and egress nodes.

RFC 4090 offers a form of segment recovery for packet MPLS-TE networks through its one-to-one detour and facility bypass methods. Neither supports the full set of RFC 4872 recovery types, and the facility method does not apply to most non-packet (non-PSC) switching technologies.

This RFC brings the full set of recovery types to a segment, meaning a portion of the LSP. It lets an upstream node signal the desired protection type, optionally say where protection starts and stops, optionally name the hops of the protection segment, and learn which paths protect an LSP. Segments can protect against any number of nodes and links, may overlap, and may be nested. The extensions are meant to be compatible with fast reroute.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you cannot plan a whole second trip, but you can plan a detour around one trouble spot. This note teaches routers how to set up and use those detours.

sections.title: Segment Recovery Concepts
sections.content:
Take the topology A-B-C-D-E-F with a side route C-G-I-E. An LSP from A to F cannot be protected end to end here, but a recovery LSP along [C,G,I,E] protects the spans {C,D} and {D,E} and node D. This is called segment protection or segment restoration, and together segment recovery.

The node that starts a recovery LSP (C in the example) is the branch node, the same role as the point of local repair in RFC 4090. The node that ends it (E) is the merge node. Each segment recovery LSP is signaled as an independent LSP: its Sender_Template carries the branch node's address and its Session object carries the merge node's address. Intermediate nodes use standard signaling, and a recovery LSP can itself be protected by segment or end-to-end recovery.

The three protection forms (1+1 unidirectional, 1+1 bidirectional, 1:1 with extra-traffic) and three re-routing and restoration forms (re-routing without extra-traffic, shared-mesh restoration, full LSP re-routing) behave like their end-to-end counterparts, except that they cover only part of the working LSP. The type to use is given to the recovery LSP's ingress in a new protection subobject.

Recovery LSPs are tied to the LSP they protect with the ASSOCIATION object from RFC 4872, and several recovery-type ASSOCIATION objects may appear on one LSP. This RFC adds Association Type value 2, Resource Sharing, which lets LSPs share resources during make-before-break even when an LSP endpoint changes. The association ID MAY be the working LSP's LSP ID, and a Resource Sharing association SHOULD NOT be removed once included.
sections.eli5: The spot where the detour leaves the main road is the branch node, and the spot where it rejoins is the merge node. A little tag on both roads says they belong together.

sections.title: Explicit Control with SERO Objects
sections.content:
An upstream node, usually the ingress, can name the branch and merge nodes using a Secondary Explicit Route object (SERO). It has the same format as an ERO, with object class 200, and it travels in Path messages. More than one SERO MAY be present, and the decision to create one is a local matter.

An SERO SHOULD hold at least three subobjects. The first MUST be the branch node, the second SHOULD be a new protection subobject (subobject type 37) saying what protection or restoration to provide, and the last MUST be the merge node. Ordinary ERO subobjects, strict or loose, MAY sit in between. The protection subobject is not valid in EROs or RROs.

A node that is not a branch node MUST pass all SEROs on unchanged. A branch node clones the Path message of the protected LSP to build the recovery LSP's Path message, with these changes:

  • The Sender_Template uses a local address and a new LSP ID.
  • The Session uses the merge node's address as the tunnel endpoint, and the extended tunnel ID is set to the local node address.
  • The PROTECTION object is replaced from the protection subobject, with the R-bit reset.
  • Incoming RROs and EROs are dropped, and a new ERO is built from the SERO that named this node, which is itself omitted.
sections.eli5: The planner writes a note that says: leave at this junction, take this kind of detour, rejoin at that junction. The junction node reads the note and builds the detour.

sections.title: Failures, Teardown and Notification
sections.content:
When a recovery LSP fails, a branch node first applies standard PathErr rules. It SHOULD also send a PathErr upstream for the protected LSP with the error "Routing Problem/LSP Segment Protection Failed" (error value 21), including an SERO that matches the failed branch. Whether path state is removed depends on the R-bit (Required) of the protected LSP's PROTECTION object. If R is set and the recovery LSP's state was removed, the upstream PathErr MUST have Path_State_Removed set, all path state for the protected LSP is removed, and PathTear goes downstream on all active branches.

Resv messages from recovery LSPs normally do not trigger upstream Resv messages, which wait for the protected LSP's Resv. ADMIN_STATUS changes are relayed by a branch node on every recovery LSP. Teardown follows standard RSVP-TE procedures, with the branch node relaying PathTear on every recovery LSP. Tearing down a recovery LSP from a non-ingress node in a non-graceful way is NOT RECOMMENDED because it can remove the protected LSP.

Notification is also changed. Branch and merge nodes SHOULD add a NOTIFY_REQUEST object for the recovery LSP and the protected LSP, listed first, so that several objects can form an ordered list. This changes RFC 3473 Section 4.2.1: instead of ignoring later NOTIFY_REQUEST objects, nodes MUST propagate them in the order received. A branch or merge node that cannot recover from a failure MUST notify the node named in the first NOTIFY_REQUEST object it received.
sections.eli5: If a detour cannot be built, the junction sends word back up the road. Depending on a flag set at the start, either the whole trip is cancelled or the main road is left alone.

sections.title: Recording Segments with SRRO Objects
sections.content:
A Secondary Record Route object (SRRO) records the path used by a recovery LSP. It has the format of a RECORD_ROUTE object, with object class 201, and it can also carry the protection subobject. Transit nodes MUST pass received SRROs on unchanged.

In Path messages, the merge node copies the RRO it received for the recovery LSP (plus any SRROs) into a new SRRO on the outgoing Path message of the recovered LSP. In Resv messages, the branch node does the same with the RRO from the recovery LSP's Resv. The Resv SRRO SHOULD start with the local node address, followed by a protection subobject holding the recovery LSP's PROTECTION object contents. Collection is requested with the segment-recording-desired flag in SESSION_ATTRIBUTE, which MAY be set even when SEROs are not used.

If an SRRO makes a Resv message too large, subobjects SHOULD be removed. The first two and the last subobject MUST NOT be removed, and the subobject after a removed one MUST be updated with the L-bit set. If the message is still too large, whole SRROs SHOULD be removed.
sections.eli5: As each detour is built, the nodes write down the route it took, so the people at the start of the trip can see exactly where every detour goes.

sections.title: Dynamic Control with PROTECTION Flags
sections.content:
Instead of naming branch and merge nodes, an upstream node can set the LSP Segment Recovery Flags in the PROTECTION object (class 37, C-Type 2) and let downstream nodes find them. The 6-bit Seg.Flags field uses the same values as the LSP Flags of RFC 4872. Two new bits are added: In-Place (I) says the requested recovery type is already in place, and Required (R) says that failing to establish the protection should fail the protected LSP. A value of zero means no dynamic identification is wanted.

A transit node that sees non-zero flags and a clear In-Place bit SHOULD check whether it can offer the recovery type and find a suitable merge node. It MUST NOT do this when an SERO already names it as a branch node. If it cannot, it processes the Path message normally and MUST NOT change the flags.

A node that identifies itself as a branch node builds the recovery LSP much as in explicit control, but sets the In-Place bit in the new PROTECTION object, and in the original one while the recovery LSP exists. The new ERO MAY come from locally computed paths. The merge node SHOULD reset In-Place in the outgoing Path message. Unlike explicit control, if a dynamically identified recovery LSP cannot be created, it is removed and no error is sent upstream.
sections.eli5: Here the planner just says: please add detours wherever you can. Routers that can help pick their own junctions and quietly skip it if they cannot.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC adds new message objects to GMPLS signaling but no new signaling messages, and it does not change the relationship between control-plane neighbors.

SEROs and SRROs mean signaling messages carry more information about LSP paths than plain EROs and RROs. Someone intercepting a message could deduce slightly more about the network, which the authors judge a very minor risk because the same information is already available via routing. Otherwise the RFC adds no security considerations and points to RFC 3473.
sections.eli5: The notes about detours tell a little more about the roads, but that was already public, so it is not a big secret.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned Association Type 2 (Resource Sharing) in the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry. In the RSVP parameters registry, SECONDARY_EXPLICIT_ROUTE was created as class 200 and SECONDARY_RECORD_ROUTE as class 201, both in the 11bbbbbb range, with the same C-Types as EXPLICIT_ROUTE and RECORD_ROUTE. The protection subobject is type 37 in both.

A new error value, 21 "LSP Segment Protection Failed", was added under the "Routing Problem" error code. The bits this RFC defines in the PROTECTION object's reserved field need no IANA action because RFC 4872 requested no registry for them.
sections.eli5: The numbers for the new objects and the new error are written in the official list so everyone uses the same ones.
